answer: A claim begins with a placard: the applicant plants a numbered board on a distinct named landmark, ties it off with a sable cord, sets an opal chip in a dated ivory frame beside it, and films the scene while a licensed witness signs the claim. The registry fingerprints each film perceptually and refuses frames already claimed. Landmark licences are auctioned in fixed lots per district, so crowding one square lifts the price of the next licence while a second seat in the same square dies on a duplicate frame. Cloning then costs dearer ground and scarcer witnesses every time.
